prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We construct a simple thermodynamic model to describe the melting of a supported metal nanoparticle with a spherically curved free surface both with and without surface melting. We use the model to investigate the results of recent molecular dynamics simulations, which suggest the melting temperature of a supported metal particle is the same as that of a free spherical particle with the same surface curvature. Our model shows that this is only the case when the contact angles of the supported solid and liquid particles are similar. This is also the case for the temperature at which surface melting begins.

outputs.L1: We develop a simple thermodynamic model to describe the melting of a supported metal nanoparticle with a spherically curved free surface, both with and without surface melting. We use this model to examine recent molecular dynamics simulations suggesting that the melting temperature of a supported metal particle is identical to that of a free spherical particle with the same surface curvature. Our model demonstrates that this equivalence holds only when the supported solid and liquid particles have similar contact angles. The same condition applies to the temperature at which surface melting begins.
outputs.L2: We develop a basic thermodynamic framework for the melting behavior of a substrate-supported metal nanoparticle whose exposed surface is spherical, considering scenarios both with and without premelting at the surface. The framework is applied to assess recent molecular dynamics findings indicating that a supported particle melts at the same temperature as an unsupported spherical particle with equivalent surface curvature. According to our analysis, this equivalence holds only when the solid and molten supported particles have approximately equal contact angles. The same requirement applies to the onset temperature of surface melting.
outputs.L3:
A simple thermodynamic model can be used to describe the melting behavior of a supported metal nanoparticle with a spherically curved free surface. The model considers two possible melting mechanisms: direct melting of the entire particle and melting preceded by the formation of a liquid surface layer.

Recent molecular dynamics simulations have suggested that a supported nanoparticle and a free spherical particle with the same surface curvature should melt at the same temperature. However, the thermodynamic analysis shows that this equivalence is not universal. It holds only when the contact angles of the supported particle in its solid and liquid states are sufficiently similar. If these contact angles differ significantly, interactions with the supporting substrate alter the melting temperature, even when the free-surface curvature matches that of a free particle.

An analogous condition governs the onset of surface melting. The temperature at which a liquid layer first forms on the supported solid particle is comparable to that of a free spherical particle with the same curvature only when the relevant solid and liquid contact angles are similar. Thus, surface curvature alone does not fully determine either the melting temperature or the onset of surface melting; the wetting behavior of the particle on the substrate is also essential.
outputs.L4:
A thermodynamic model is developed to describe melting in supported metal nanoparticles whose free surfaces are curved. Both direct melting and melting preceded by the formation of a liquid surface layer are considered. The model accounts for the interfacial free energies of the solid particle, liquid particle, substrate, and surrounding medium, as well as the different contact angles adopted by the solid and liquid phases on the support. It is used to evaluate molecular-dynamics predictions that the melting behavior of a supported nanoparticle can be related to that of a free spherical particle having the same free-surface curvature.

The analysis shows that curvature alone does not generally determine the melting temperature. The substrate also affects the balance of interfacial free energies and may alter the particle geometry when the solid transforms into a liquid. Consequently, a supported particle and a free spherical particle with the same curvature can exhibit different melting temperatures. The same limitation applies to the temperature at which surface melting begins.

The curvature-based correspondence becomes valid only when the equilibrium contact angles of the supported solid and liquid are equal or sufficiently similar. Under this condition, the substrate contributes almost equally to the free energies of the two phases, and its effect largely cancels in the melting equilibrium. The melting temperature and the onset temperature for surface melting then coincide with those predicted for a free spherical particle of the same curvature. If the contact angles differ substantially, however, the support must be included explicitly, and comparison based solely on surface curvature is not reliable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a paper presenting a thermodynamic model of melting in supported metal nanoparticles, including surface melting, curvature effects, molecular dynamics comparisons, and the role of solid and liquid contact angles.
counterfactuals.output: We present a thermodynamic model for melting in supported metal nanoparticles that incorporates surface premelting, curvature-dependent interfacial energetics, and substrate interactions. The framework predicts particle-size-dependent melting temperatures, liquid-shell formation, and the evolution of solid and liquid regions during melting. Comparison with molecular dynamics simulations shows that accounting for both curvature effects and surface melting improves agreement over classical capillarity models. The analysis further demonstrates that the solid and liquid contact angles independently influence melting behavior by controlling the relative substrate–particle interfacial free energies. These results provide a unified description of how particle size, morphology, wetting, and surface structure govern melting in supported nanoscale metals.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how the melting temperature of a supported metal nanoparticle compares with that of a free spherical particle having the same surface curvature.
counterfactuals.output: In the classical capillarity model, a supported metal nanoparticle has essentially the **same melting temperature as a free spherical particle with the same radius of surface curvature**. The support changes the particle’s shape and contact angle, but curvature—not total volume or footprint—sets the melting-point shift. Strong substrate interactions, strain, or interfacial reactions can cause deviations from this ideal result.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in one paragraph, under what conditions supported and free metal nanoparticles exhibit the same melting and surface-melting onset temperatures.
counterfactuals.output: Supported and free metal nanoparticles have the same melting temperature and surface-melting onset when the support is effectively thermodynamically neutral: it does not significantly change particle size or shape, impose strain, transfer charge, cause alloying or interdiffusion, or alter atomic mobility, and it stabilizes the solid and liquid phases equally. Formally, the substrate contributions to the solid and liquid interfacial free energies must cancel—so replacing a free surface with a particle–support interface does not change the solid–liquid free-energy balance—and the exposed surfaces must retain the same structure and energies as those of the free particle. This limit is approached for weakly interacting, inert, nonwetting supports and otherwise identical, equilibrated nanoparticles.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract about a simple thermodynamic model for supported nanoparticles with spherically curved free surfaces, both with and without surface melting.
counterfactuals.output: We present a simple thermodynamic model for supported nanoparticles with spherically curved free surfaces, considering both fully solid particles and particles covered by a molten surface layer. The model combines bulk free energies with solid–vapor, liquid–vapor, solid–liquid, and particle–substrate interfacial contributions, while accounting for curvature-induced pressure and substrate wetting through the equilibrium contact geometry. Minimization of the total Gibbs free energy determines the stable particle shape, phase state, and—when surface melting is allowed—the thickness of the liquid shell as functions of particle size and temperature. For particles without surface melting, the model recovers the curvature-driven depression of the melting temperature, modified by adhesion to the support. When surface melting is included, a liquid layer can become favorable below the complete melting temperature and grow continuously or discontinuously depending on the balance of interfacial energies. The substrate may either promote or suppress premelting by altering the energetic competition among the free surface, solid–liquid interface, and particle–support contact. The framework provides transparent scaling relations for size-dependent melting and clarifies how curvature, wetting, and adhesion jointly govern the thermal stability of supported nanoparticles.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you describe a theoretical investigation that tests molecular dynamics claims about curvature-controlled melting in supported metal particles and identifies contact-angle similarity as the key condition?
counterfactuals.output:
A suitable investigation would use a capillarity-based thermodynamic model to test the molecular-dynamics claim that the melting temperature of a supported metal nanoparticle is determined solely by its surface curvature.

The solid and liquid particles are treated as equilibrium spherical caps of fixed atom number on a flat substrate. For each phase \(i=s,l\), the free energy is written as

\[
G_i=N\mu_i(T)+\gamma_{iv}A_{iv}
+\left(\gamma_{i\mathrm{sub}}-\gamma_{\mathrm{sub},v}\right)A_{i\mathrm{sub}},
\]

with the cap geometry constrained by the corresponding Young contact angle,

\[
\gamma_{\mathrm{sub},v}-\gamma_{i\mathrm{sub}}
=\gamma_{iv}\cos\theta_i .
\]

Equating the solid and liquid free energies gives the size-dependent melting temperature. The calculation can then be repeated over particle size and substrate interaction strength and compared with MD results, especially by plotting melting-point depression against inverse free-surface radius, \(1/R\).

The analysis shows that a curvature-only Gibbs–Thomson description is not generally valid for supported particles. It emerges when the equilibrium solid and liquid have the same, or nearly the same, contact angle:

\[
\theta_s \simeq \theta_l .
\]

Under this condition, the substrate-related surface terms and spherical-cap shape factors largely cancel between the two phases. The melting-point shift then scales approximately with mean curvature,

\[
T_m(R)\approx T_m^\infty\left(1-\frac{C}{R}\right),
\]

so particles with different supports or apparent shapes collapse onto a common curvature-based relation.

If \(\theta_s\) and \(\theta_l\) differ appreciably, melting entails a change in wetted area and particle shape. The associated substrate and interfacial free-energy change contributes independently to the transition, so particles with the same curvature need not melt at the same temperature. Thus the investigation would qualify the MD claim: **curvature controls supported-particle melting only when the solid and liquid exhibit contact-angle similarity; that similarity, rather than support independence itself, is the key condition.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
